subject: Historia
title: The Viking Age and Sweden's Middle Ages
sourceSummary: Viking trade, travel and society, runestones as a historical source, the Christianisation of Sweden, how the country gradually became a kingdom, and the Kalmar Union.
topics: the Viking Age as a period
Sweden's Middle Ages and the Kalmar Union

questions.topic: the Viking Age as a period
questions.prompt: When is the Viking Age in the Nordic region usually dated to?
questions.opener: The period ends the Iron Age and gives way to the Middle Ages.
choices: Roughly 200-500 AD
Roughly 500-800 AD
Roughly 800-1050 AD
Roughly 1200-1500 AD
questions.explanation: The Viking Age is usually dated from around 800 to around 1050, by which point Christianity and royal power had become established and the Middle Ages had begun in the Nordic region. The period 1200-1500 is already Swedish medieval times, not the Viking Age.

questions.prompt: Where did Vikings from present-day Sweden mainly travel to trade?
questions.opener: Think about the rivers heading east and a great city known as Miklagard.
choices: West to Greenland and North America
East along the rivers through what is now Russia, all the way to Miklagard (Constantinople)
South around Africa
North over the North Pole
questions.explanation: Vikings from Svealand travelled mainly eastward, along rivers such as the Volga and the Dnieper, trading furs, iron and slaves for silver and silk - thousands of Arab silver coins have been found in Swedish soil. Voyages to Greenland and North America were mainly made by Norwegians and Icelanders, and no one sailed around Africa until the 1400s.

questions.opener: The site lies on Björkö in Lake Mälaren and is still being excavated by archaeologists.
choices: An important trading centre on Lake Mälaren during the Viking Age
A medieval castle in Skåne
A royal grave in Uppsala
A Viking Age law about inheritance
questions.explanation: Birka on Björkö was Sweden's most important trading town during the 8th and 9th centuries, where goods and coins from both Western Europe and the Orient have been found in graves and refuse layers. It was therefore a trading centre, not a castle, a grave or a law.

questions.prompt: Why are runestones a valuable source of knowledge about the Viking Age?
questions.opener: Think about when the stones were made in relation to the events they describe.
choices: They contain complete history books about the whole of the Nordic region
They were written by monks much later and are therefore reliable
They are painted pictures of Viking ships
They are contemporary sources, carved by people who lived at the time, and tell of people, journeys and beliefs
questions.explanation: Runestones were raised during the Viking Age itself and the early Middle Ages, usually as memorials to someone who had died, and their short texts mention names, family ties, journeys and sometimes Christian faith. That makes them contemporary sources. The texts, however, are very short - a few lines, not whole history books - and they were written by Norse people themselves, not by later monks.

questions.opener: He is usually mentioned as the first in a long line of Christian Swedish kings.
choices: A monk who wrote Sweden's first law
The first Swedish king to be baptised as a Christian, around the year 1000
A Danish king who conquered Sweden
The leader of the Hanseatic League in Visby
questions.explanation: Olof Skötkonung is considered to be the first Swedish king who was Christian and was baptised, according to tradition at Husaby in Västergötland around the year 1000. Christianisation nevertheless proceeded slowly and took a further hundred years or more before it was complete across the whole country - he was therefore neither a monk, a Danish king, nor a trade leader.

questions.topic: Sweden's Middle Ages and the Kalmar Union
questions.prompt: What was the Kalmar Union, formed in 1397?
questions.opener: Three Nordic kingdoms, one and the same monarch.
choices: A trade agreement between Kalmar and Lübeck
A new law code for the whole Nordic region
A union in which Denmark, Norway and Sweden shared the same monarch
An alliance between Sweden and Germany against Russia
questions.explanation: In Kalmar in 1397, Eric of Pomerania was crowned king over Denmark, Norway and Sweden, a union that Queen Margaret had worked to bring about. The countries kept their own laws and councils but shared a monarch. The union was marked by recurring conflicts and effectively broke up when Gustav Vasa became king of Sweden in 1523.

questions.topic: Sweden's Middle Ages and the Kalmar Union
questions.prompt: Explain step by step how Sweden went from many small provinces to becoming one kingdom.
questions.opener: Start with how power was organised during the Viking Age and then follow it forward in time.
questions.answer: During the Viking Age, Sweden consisted of provinces with their own assemblies (things) and their own laws, where chieftains and magnates held power locally. During the 11th and 12th centuries royal power grew, and Christianity gave the king the support of a church that organised the country into dioceses and parishes. During the 13th century, taxes, a common church organisation and written provincial laws were introduced, and Magnus Eriksson's national law code in the 14th century applied to the whole realm. Sweden had thereby become a kingdom with a king, a church, taxes and common laws, albeit with continued strong provincial rule.
steps: The Viking Age: the provinces governed themselves through assemblies, and power lay with local magnates.
Royal power grew as a king was able to demand tax and military service from several provinces.
Christianisation gave the king the church's support, and the country was divided into dioceses and parishes with bishops and priests.
During the 13th century the provincial laws were written down and a firmer system of tax collection was built up.
In the 14th century the realm got a common law for the whole country, and Sweden then entered the Kalmar Union in 1397.

questions.prompt: Summarise the Viking Age and Sweden's path to becoming a medieval kingdom.
questions.opener: Take travel and trade, society, sources, Christianisation and the union in turn.
questions.answer: Viking Age: c. 800-1050, ends the Iron Age in the Nordic region · Travel: Swedish Vikings travelled mainly eastward along the rivers through what is now Russia to Miklagard (Constantinople), Norwegians and Icelanders westward to Iceland, Greenland and North America, Danes and Norwegians towards England and France · Trade: furs, iron, hides and slaves were exchanged for silver, silk and glass - thousands of Arab silver coins have been found in Swedish soil · Trading centres: Birka on Lake Mälaren, later Sigtuna and Visby · Society: most people were farmers, assemblies (things) made decisions and passed judgment, society was divided into magnates, free farmers and thralls · Runestones: contemporary sources, usually memorial stones with short texts about names, family, journeys and beliefs · Christianisation: Ansgar visited Birka in the 9th century, Olof Skötkonung was baptised around the year 1000, the process took over a hundred years · Sweden's Middle Ages: royal power, church organisation, taxes and provincial laws built a kingdom · Kalmar Union 1397: Denmark, Norway and Sweden under the same monarch, driven forward by Queen Margaret, broke up in practice with Gustav Vasa in 1523.
